title: Why Songs Get Stuck
objective: After this level you can explain why some songs get stuck in your head.
summary: About 9 in 10 people get a weekly earworm, usually a looping snippet. Sticky tunes are faster, with a familiar shape and one odd leap. Listening, distraction or gum can help.

cards.headline: About 9 in 10 people get a song stuck in their head every week.
cards.body: That's from a survey of more than 12,000 people in Finland. Scientists call it involuntary musical imagery; everyone else calls it an earworm. So why does one tune move in and refuse to leave, while another never visits at all?

cards.headline: It's a loop, not a song
cards.body: Notice what actually plays in your head. It's rarely the whole track, start to finish. Most earworms are short snippets of a larger tune, a line or two that ends and starts again. That's part of why they're so hard to shake: a snippet has no ending to wrap things up, so round it goes, like a GIF of a song.

cards.headline: The recipe for a sticky tune
cards.body: In 2016, researchers asked 3,000 people which songs got stuck in their heads, then compared those songs with similarly popular ones nobody named. The earworms tended to be faster. Their melodies had a common overall shape, Level 5's contour, the kind your ear already knows. And they had something unusual too: a surprising leap or repetition. Familiar shape, one odd twist: that's the hook that catches.

cards.fact: The song people named most often: Lady Gaga's "Bad Romance."
cards.context: Next came Journey's "Don't Stop Believin'" and Kylie Minogue's "Can't Get You Out of My Head", a title that doubles as a confession. Sorry if one of them just moved in.

cards.headline: How to evict one
cards.body: In a 2014 study, the most popular and effective responses were surprisingly simple: listen to the tune itself, or distract yourself with other music or with words. Another option came from a 2015 University of Reading study: chew gum. It cut down on stuck songs, likely because chewing keeps busy the mouth-movement planning you use to sing a tune silently in your head.

mascot.line: Some of that silent singing seems to lean on your mouth's planning. Gum gives it other work.

questions.prompt: In a survey of more than 12,000 people in Finland, how many reported an earworm at least once a week?

options.label: About half
options.rationale: Closer, but the share was higher.

questions.explanation: About 9 in 10 people reported involuntary musical imagery, an earworm, at least weekly.

questions.prompt: Based on the 2016 study of 3,000 people's stuck songs, which new song is most likely to become an earworm?

options.rationale: Earworms had a common overall shape.

options.rationale: Stuck tunes tend to be snippets that loop.

questions.prompt: The earworm study found sticky songs share a common contour. From Level 5, what is a melody's contour?

options.label: The words that go with it
options.rationale: The same contour can carry different words.

options.label: Its overall shape as it rises and falls

questions.explanation: Contour is the shape a melody traces as it rises, falls or arches, and earworms tend to have familiar ones.
